messages.subject: absurdly large mi
parts:
I apologize in advance for the complicated model and large dataset which are attached to this email. I can't figure out why I am getting a single absurdly large modification index for tot_abun_log ~~ iso_reg_mean when I use the function modificationIndices() on the fitted model object. Any insight here would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,

-Jes

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: absurdly large mi
parts:
On 03/21/2014 08:22 PM, Jes Coyle wrote:
> I apologize in advance for the complicated model and large dataset which
> are attached to this email. I can't figure out why I am getting a single
> absurdly large modification index for tot_abun_log ~~ iso_reg_mean when
> I use the function modificationIndices() on the fitted model object. Any
> insight here would be greatly appreciated.

You can safely ignore it. It is (I think) one of those
covariances/correlations that does not make sense anyway: iso_reg_mean
is an exogenous variable, while tot_abun_log is (also) an endogenous
variable. It has no meaning.

What lavaan should do, is simply not to report them in the output of
modindices().

Yves.

messages.author: c1e1212cf2e076c1
messages.subject: Re: absurdly large mi
parts:
First of all cheers for providing the workable example. I had to make only minor changes to the R script to make it run fine.

A couple of comments about the initial model it produces. You notice all fit indices are not promising - RMSEA=0.1, CFI/TLI are under 0.9. You also have some items with low loadings: a6 loads under 0.3 on ct1. These are going to be signs that you have parameters that are not "correctly" specified. You'll notice the first 3 modindices all pertain to item a6, which has that low loading. The epc for the mod on dm, and negative for the mods on as and ct2.

Another interesting thing here is the correlation matrix of the factors (I say correlation because you've fixed the variances to 1 I believe), obtained via 
inspect(fitcfa1,"coef")$psi

Obtains negative relationships between dm and ct2 and as. Right now a6 loads low on ct1, which has a positive correlation with dm, none with ct1, and positive with as. This correlation structure looks a little odd - and could be driven by the misplacement of a6.

Look what happens when you respecify the model following the modindices - make a6 load on ct2 and as. Fit stats are slightly better (though not drastically); a6 still loads low on the two other factors, so again you may want to adjust. Even consider removing entirely - if you try that, the fit stats actually improve slightly more. The largest modindices now don't have a6 in them. Run an EFA using factanal(data,factors=4) and you'll see that a6 doesn't load with a7 and a8.

You still have high modindices and poor fit, so you need to make further adjustments to your model. Keep in mind, though, once you start making tons of changes to your model, your theory gets called into question.

Not knowing anything about what you are modeling, here are some thoughts:
- Are you modeling ill-defined or relatively broad constructs? It could be that a small number of items per construct isn't enough to really establish that you are measuring anything.
- Are your items truly conceptually aligned? Maybe there is something missing among them?

In general I have found that modeling with categorical and dichotomous variables, because the variability is less, sometimes you have to do a lot more "thinking" about your model.

parts:
Dear Robin,

Many thanks for your advice, I really appreciate it!

Regarding your question, I would like to explain some topics:

The research is about an structure detection of an scale related to demand control support in a specific population
(Attached is an article that used the method that I am trying to reproduce)

First I run an EFA:

m4<- cbind(aa1,aa2,aa3,aa4,aa5,aa6,aa7,aa8,aa9,aa10,aa11,aa12,aa13,aa14,aa15,aa16,aa17)

fit1<-fa.poly(m4,nfactors=4,n.obs = 842, n.iter=1, residuals=TRUE,rotate="geominQ", min.err = .001, max.iter=50, symmetric=TRUE, warnings=TRUE,
fm="wlsmv",alpha=.05, p =.05,score="regression",weight=NULL,global=TRUE)
print(fit1)

I chose this method (WLSMV estimator and geomin oblique rotation) because the data are ordinal (Likert scale) and it is expected that items are correlated.

The model fitted in CFA was built based on the results of this analysis.

I am thinking in fit a CFA model just with items that have factor loadings upper to 0.30. Although, in this case, the item aa6, that seems to be "problematic", remains in ct1 factor.

Maybe, observations of modindices that you made can help me justify removing (entirely) item 6.

I worry about factors with only two items, but I think I can't group correlated factors because it disagrees with the theoretical construct of the scale.Do you have some opinion on this?

Any idea would be much appreciated!

Kind regards,
Hellen

messages.author: c1e1212cf2e076c1
messages.subject: Re: absurdly large mi
parts:
I've actually read this paper before.

2 items per factor is kind of rough, but in this case it is identifiable because of items you have. If you were to just model that one factor without the rest of the items in the correlation matrix, you'd have to constrain more parameters in the model. You also may not have very high reliability on this particular factor (I would use multidimensional omega in this case, in the paper you cite they call it composite reliability - they cite Fornell & Larcker, I would also cite Raykov and MacDonald). I'd also point out that the ct2 factor only has 2 as well.

It is interesting that your model doesn't track that close to their model on all of the factors. If your data were collected in a high quality fashion and the instrument was the same as what they used, then this would be an interesting finding worthy of publication I think. You may even want to communicate with the authors, maybe they can provide some insight as to why your model is different. Your model fit - though not great - isn't that far of what is reported in the paper, and if you remove a6 it is better than what they reported.

Regarding your comment about the the 0.3 cutoff for relevant items - I think that is relative to your model. If your loadings are well higher than that, then a6 loading at 0.3 seems like it doesn't belong. Given the high mod index, I think you are justified from a statistical standpoint in removing it. From the conceptual side, it may be necessary to keep that item in your model, but in that case I would consider reworking it into your model better. Remember, just because model fit has numbers doesn't mean that is all you need to consider. Model fit is only as good as the models you compare it to.

A couple things you may want to think about: explore correlations among residuals. This would violate local independence, and indicate that there may be something else going on, perhaps another factor or some cross-loadings. Keep in mind, cross-loadings may or may not be acceptable depending on what you are trying to do. Based on how this paper uses the F&L framework for divergent/convergent validity among the factors, it looks like that isn't something you would want.

messages.subject: Re: absurdly large mi
parts:
Local independence ive seen most often brought up in the context of item response theory or rasch modeling - if you google that im sure you can find all sorts of resources and explanations as to why it is important from a measurement perspective. 


To test for local independence you can look at the correlations of all items, not just those that losd on the same factor. Think about them differently as you evaluate the output. If residuals across different factors are correlated that means you may have an item that should load on more than one factor (and the mod index should point that out as well). If thats the case you could have a discrimant validity issue- your model doesnt cleanly differentiate among the factors because your items are cross loading. Not everyone sees this as a problem but rasch modelers probably would. If you have correlated residuals of items in the sames factor that is whewre local independence is violated - that means there is something going on with those items that is not shared with the other items. 

As you assess the correlations look at both statistical significance and magnitude. Depending on your sample size they could all come up as significant, but they may be too small to worry about. I dont really know how sample size in an ordinal cfa plays in to the residual estimation so i cant really comment on the specifics of that aspect.
